body:
`FourierTridiagonalPoissonSolver` set the mean of its solution to zero with `ϕ .= ϕ .- mean(ϕ)` after the backward transforms, which copies the mean to the host (a device synchronization per solve) and streams the whole complex field twice. The column at zero wavenumber in both transformed directions holds the horizontal mean of the solution at every level, so the gauge is now applied to that column before the backward transforms, with a `sum(column, dims=1)` that stays on the device.

- Results agree with `main` to 3e-16 relative for all three tridiagonal directions, bounded and periodic transformed directions, and a `Flat` direction. The stretched-grid Poisson tests now also check that the solution has zero mean.
- One solve on an H100 with a stretched grid takes 0.106 ms instead of 0.133 ms at 64³, and 8.26 ms instead of 9.60 ms at 512²×256.

Addresses point 1 of the write-up in https://github.com/CliMA/Oceananigans.jl/pull/6166#issuecomment-6041901724.

body:
*Update: I've finalized the configuration for this PR and is now ready to review. Refer to this benchmark https://github.com/CliMA/Oceananigans.jl/pull/6171#issuecomment-6222283735 as the final version. We get about 75% improvement on the PCG algorithm!*

---

The `ConjugateGradientPoissonSolver` iteration streams every field several times and runs five full-array reductions through the generic `mapreducedim!`. This PR accumulates the reductions in the Laplacian and update kernels and computes every scalar (α, β, the gauge means) on the device. The algorithm, gauge and convergence criterion are unchanged. Without a preconditioner, an iteration goes from 22 full-array passes and 5 full reductions to 11 passes and 2 short reductions, and a time step runs 1.8–6.1× faster on an H100. It builds on #6086 and #6166.

## How

The gauge needs the means of the updated `x` and `r`, and these are known before the fields are written:

$$
\Sigma (x + \alpha p) = \Sigma x + \alpha \Sigma p, \qquad \Sigma (r - \alpha q) = \Sigma r - \alpha \Sigma q .
$$

Below, every field under `reads` or `writes` is one full-array pass, $\Sigma$ sums over the active cells, $\chi$ is the active-cell mask, $N = \Sigma \chi$, and `M` stands for the preconditioner's passes.

**`main`**, one iteration:

```
                                             reads    writes   passes   reductions
z   = M r                     precondition!                         M
ρ   = z ⋅ r                   dot!           z, r                   2            1
p   = z + β p                 broadcast      z, p     p             3
q   = A p                     Laplacian      p        q             2
pᵀq = p ⋅ q                   dot!           p, q                   2            1
α   = ρ / pᵀq
x   = x + α p                 broadcast      x, p     x             3
r   = r - α q                 broadcast      r, q     r             3
Σx  = Σ x                     sum!           x                      1            1
Σr  = Σ r                     sum!           r                      1            1
x   = (x - Σx/N) χ            gauge kernel   x        x             2
r   = (r - Σr/N) χ                           r        r             2
‖V⁻¹r‖                        norm           r                      1            1
                                                               22 + M            5
```

**This PR**, one iteration ($\Sigma x$ and $\Sigma r$ come from the previous update kernel):

```
                                             reads    writes   passes   reductions
z   = M r                     precondition!                         M
ρ   = z ⋅ r                   column kernel  z, r                   2        short
p   = z + β p                 search kernel  z, p     p             3
      β = ρ / ρⁱ⁻¹
Laplacian kernel, per cell:
    q    = A p                               p        q             2
    pᵀq += p q,  Σp += p,  Σq += q                                           short
update kernel:
    α = ρ / pᵀq,  x̄ = (Σx + α Σp) / N,  r̄ = (Σr - α Σq) / N,  ρⁱ⁻¹ = ρ
    per cell:
    x    = (x + α p - x̄) χ                   x, p     x             3
    r    = (r - α q - r̄) χ                   r, q     r             3
    Σx += x,  Σr += r,  rᵀr += r r,  ‖V⁻¹r‖² += (r/V)²                       short
                                                               13 + M      3 short
```

Without a preconditioner `z` is `r` and $\rho$ is the `rᵀr` from the previous update kernel, which gives 11 passes and 2 short reductions per iteration against 22 and 5 on `main`.

The kernels launch in one dimension over column segments, sized so a launch has about $2^{20}$ threads. Each workgroup adds its threads' sums in local memory, and a single workgroup adds the workgroups' sums in a fixed order, so the reduction is deterministic and allocates nothing. On `Distributed` architectures, `reduce_partial_sums!` adds the ranks' sums with one `Allreduce`.

The fused path applies to what `ConjugateGradientPoissonSolver` builds by default (`compute_symmetric_laplacian!`, `ZeroMeanGaugeCondition`, `VolumeInverseNorm`) with any preconditioner. Everything else keeps the generic `iterate!`, which is unchanged. The update kernel writes the interior of `x` only, not its halos, which nothing reads. Once the residual is `NaN`, the fused `iterating` returns `false` and the solve stops, where the generic one iterates to `maxiter`.

## Equivalence

The fused and unfused versions agree to summation-order roundoff with identical iteration counts, on 1 and 8 H100s and on 1 and 2 CPU ranks, with no preconditioner, the FFT preconditioner and `DiagonallyDominantPreconditioner`. `test/poisson_solvers/conjugate_gradient.jl` passes on CPU and H100, and the `distributed_solvers` MPI group passes on 4 ranks.

## Performance

Time step speedup over `main`, one H100:

| case | no preconditioner | FFT preconditioner |
|---|---|---|
| 64³ (CI benchmark) | 6.1× | 2.8× |
| rough Rayleigh–Bénard, 320 × 320 × 2560 | 1.8× | 1.07× |
| staircase convection, 192 × 192 × 1536 | 2.2× | 1.13× |
| vortex sheet, 8000 × 4000 | 2.2× | 1.13× |

With the FFT preconditioner on large grids the FFT solve is 75–87% of an iteration, which this PR leaves alone. Computing α and β in the kernels removes a further 60 launches per time step at 64³.

## Future improvements

- Accumulate $\rho = z \cdot r$ in each preconditioner's final kernel, removing the column-dot pass on the preconditioned path.
- Single-reduction CG (Chronopoulos and Gear 1989) or pipelined CG (Ghysels and Vanroose 2014) merge the two remaining synchronizations, at the cost of an extra field and some attainable accuracy.
- Add each workgroup's sums with a tree. A few threads add all 256 values, which is the likely reason wide grids run behind one thread per column with a `sum!`: 14.0 vs 12.6 ms per unpreconditioned iteration on 1280 × 1280 × 160.
- The $2^{20}$-thread target was measured on an H100. GPUs with more memory bandwidth need more threads in flight and may want a larger target.

Fusing the inner products into the vector updates is established for CG on GPUs (Aliaga et al. 2013, [slides](https://www.hpca.uji.es/wp-content/uploads/recent_talks/aliaga/ICPP_2013.pdf); Rupp et al. 2016, [doi](https://doi.org/10.1145/2907944)), and MITgcm's `cg2d` (Marshall et al. 1997, [doi](https://doi.org/10.1029/96JC02775)) does the same across ranks with one `GLOBAL_SUM`.
